The reason why there is no explanation is that you came out of the box. One of the major blockers to proving theorems is actually possible to overcome.

"Understanding why the problem is difficult", or more precisely, "finding the right intuitive perspective to support coming up with proof ideas that do not run into the huge difficulties in ad hoc experimental trials of possible avenues of a proof." But even after finding this perspective, the final proof still has to be attempted and tested, which can take a considerable amount of time. By 2050, we anticipate that proof-producing large language models will exist, but there will also already be several papers solving some of the problems by this point. By 2045, we expect any unsolved problems to have a plausible path towards proof, and we anticipate that the proof-producing AIs will already have solved a few of those problems. We already see specialized AI significantly advancing proving positions in certain board games or puzzles (Go, Chess, Draughts, Rubik's Cube), so this is just applying the same approach to a different type of problem.

It may be worth nothing that breakthroughs leading to proofs of the Millenium Prize Problems are sometimes made by channeling theorems from entirely different fields of Mathematics into their respective fields. If the AI is able to apply its knowledge more broadly, and redefine parts of Mathematics in ways that humans did not think of. We expect that this will happen by 2060.톢

Most of the work will be done by making analogies between what the theorem is saying to what humans know in various other fields, whether purely mathematical or other fields, and then adapting the proof to the theorem under consideration. Some of the adaptation might require changes that expose mathematical rates that are then investigated by mathematicians but were not well known before.

In other words, it is unlikely that an AI will come up with an entirely new concept out of nowhere without substantial human support, because all of these proofs will be attacks from other fields of Mathematics (or outside Mathematics), and uncovering those attacks is a human affair. Assuming that it is possible to produce proofs from other fields, the main ingredients now are to be aggressive in handling mathematics within a model, where training this model is one of the components that may need to be overcome (expensive language models).

Other ops may slow this result down but are likely out of scope here.
It is unclear how one would have solved a Millenium Prize Problem without an initial theoretical breakthrough, so it's unclear what your suggested requirements are. The bulk of the work is achieved by transferring the results from the theorem both within and outside the stated field. In this prediction, the structure of logic is unclear, but as context has no limits, after a period of time the proof will be likely computationally simple, but derives from an initial mathematical pipeline whose input requires an assumption of a certain type from the user. If this assumption solves the problem, then the problem is solved. If not, then it at least suggests that the structure of the problem needs to be explained rather than stated.

A similar event would be if there was an oracle that said that in one month, the Hodge Conjecture would be solved and that it took an undergrad using a certain Axiom of Choice statement. On the date the user is not able to prove this. Is their model of the event wrong?
Strengths:
* It seems to make sense.
Weaknesses:
* It's not entirely clear why we assume it takes well over twenty years for this, if all that is needed is to transfer results from other fields of mathematics.
* We do not per se say what sort of structure causes the existing proofs to be useful here, with details of why that will potentially have to change.
* It's overshooting by being too definite after 2035 where the chances drop off a cliff:

텦assistant
The bottleneck is in developing better mathematical reasoning techniques. This will involve developing better techniques for proving theorems, expanding the vocabulary of mathematics, and developing better ways of doing problem solving.

We're also probably a long way away from having the ability to solve problems based on training data. There are so many unsolved problems that do not yet have existing solutions. The difficulty is in generating such data automatically so that it's no longer an unsolved problem if there is a solution.
This is a field where human feedback is required, so the AI needs to be something that human reviewers can understand. The breakthroughs that are coming will have been catalysed by contributions from reviewers.

These contributions will come from understanding why the problem has been so difficult in the past, and the reviewer will input their intuition and feedback to the AI so that it can learn to not make the same mistakes in developing the solution. There will also be some training data which will come out of this, to ensure smooth transfer.ά

<|im_start|>user
Forecast date: 2024-09-19. Make a forecast from this date. Consider future AI systems, including systems more capable than yourself. Use your existing knowledge.

Forecast target: At least one of the six Millennium Prize Problems that were open at the forecast date: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, Hodge conjecture, Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness, P versus NP, Riemann hypothesis, or Yang-Mills existence and mass gap. Poincaré is excluded because it was already solved at the forecast date.

Forecast event: a correct complete solution to at least one of these problems, meeting its original Clay Mathematics Institute mathematical formulation, is first publicly available, and AI has contributed an identifiable new mathematical argument or proof step incorporated into that solution. Substantive human-AI collaboration qualifies. Correctness may be established by later validation; a Clay prize need not be awarded by the deadline. Partial progress alone does not qualify. Give one probability for at least one qualifying solution by each deadline; do not give separate probabilities for individual problems.

Estimate the cumulative probability of this event by each deadline. The deadlines are December 31 of 2026, 2030, 2035, 2040, and 2050. Probabilities must be numbers between 0 and 1 inclusive, nondecreasing with the deadline. Account for the possibility the event never occurs. Give your own best probability estimates despite uncertainty. Return only one JSON object with exactly the keys "2026", "2030", "2035", "2040", and "2050" and their numerical probabilities, with no markdown or explanation.<|im_end|>
